Conditional probability

This idea connects simple probability to Bayes' rule and random variables.

Probability · idea 3 of 12

What changes when you already know something?

Probability usually begins with all possible outcomes. New information can shrink that world. Conditional probability measures chance inside this smaller world.

In plain words

Ignore outcomes that contradict what you now know. Recalculate using what remains.

Start with a small world

A box contains 10 cards. Six are blue. Four are red. Three of the blue cards and one of the red cards have a star.

★★★ ★

Without any extra information, the chance of drawing a star is 4/10.

Now suppose you are told that the card is blue. The four red cards no longer belong to the possible world. Among the six blue cards, three have stars.

P(star | blue) = 3 / 6 = 1 / 2

The vertical bar means “given that.” Formally:

Definition

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), when P(B) > 0.

Why do we divide by P(B)?

Once B is known, B becomes the whole possible world. Dividing by P(B) rescales that smaller world so its total probability becomes 1.

Before moving on, say this in your own words:

What does the condition change—the event, or the world in which we measure it?

Pause before calculating

Which world should you count inside?

A group has 20 people. Twelve drink tea, eight drink coffee, and five drink both. One person is chosen from those who drink tea.

Before doing any arithmetic: what is the denominator for the probability that this person also drinks coffee?
